title: The Charter of Madinah
subtitle: An early community agreement: security, faith, and the valley of Yathrib
summary: The people living in Yathrib, and the document Ibn Ishaq and Abu Ubayd preserve as the sahifah: one community, help with blood-money, the faith of the Jewish clans who joined it, defense of the valley, and the referral of disputes to God and the Messenger.

sections.text: After the mosque and the pairings among the Muslims, the Prophet addressed the rest of Yathrib. The oasis held the Muhajirun, the Aws and the Khazraj, Jewish clans including groups tied to Banu Qaynuqa, Banu al-Nadir, and Banu Qurayzah, and Arab households that had not accepted Islam.

In pre-Islamic Arabia, social order had rested solely on raw tribal kinship: an attack on a clansman demanded collective retaliation, regardless of right or wrong. Without a shared legal framework, the historical animosities of Yathrib threatened to erupt at any moment. Recognizing this vulnerability, the Prophet set down an agreement that the early historians preserve as Kitab al-Madinah or al-Sahifah. It is that document, not a constitution in the later sense of the word.
The bustling courtyards and palm architecture of ancient Madinah where civic peace was codified.
Core Principles of the Historic Document

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Ubayd, in Kitab al-Amwal, preserve an opening in this sense: this is a document from Muhammad the Prophet, between the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and of Yathrib and whoever follows them, joins them, and strives with them. They are one ummah, apart from other people. The text calls them one ummah. It does not itself use the later vocabulary of a constitution or of citizenship.

Among the clauses in that preserved text: the believers do not leave one of their number who is burdened by a debt of blood or ransom without helping him in fairness. A believer does not kill a believer in retaliation for a disbeliever, and does not help a disbeliever against a believer. The God-fearing among them stand together against whoever of them commits aggression or seeks injustice, sin, enmity, or corruption among the believers. Their hands are against him together, even if he is the son of one of them. That is a restriction, in the document, on shielding such a person. It is not a modern statute abolishing every form of collective responsibility, and this chapter does not call it that.
Freedom of Faith and the Jewish Covenant
A section concerns Jewish clans who entered the document. The wording for the Jews of Banu Awf, as Ibn Hisham and Abu Ubayd give it, is:

وَإِنَّ يَهُودَ بَنِي عَوْفٍ أُمَّةٌ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، لِلْيَهُودِ دِينُهُمْ وَلِلْمُسْلِمِينَ دِينُهُمْ، مَوَالِيهِمْ وَأَنْفُسُهُمْ
'And indeed, the Jews of Banu Awf are a community alongside the believers; the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have their religion—their clients and their own selves.' (Kitab al-Amwal by Abu Ubayd & Sirat Ibn Hisham)

The same form of words is extended in the text to other named groups, among them Banu al-Najjar, Banu al-Harith, Banu Sa'idah, Banu Jusham, Banu al-Aws, and Banu Tha'labah: the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs. The document does not list synagogues. It does say that each side bears its own expenses, and that they help one another against whoever fights the people of this document. Whoever does wrong ruins only himself and the people of his house.
The mountain valleys of Madinah that formed an inviolable sanctuary of security under the Charter.
Mutual Defense and the Rule of Law

The valley is not left without a rule of defense. The text says that the Jews spend with the believers so long as they are at war. No protection is given to Quraysh, or to anyone who helps them. The neighbor who is under protection is as one's own person, and is not to be harmed. These are provisions of the document as the early historians transmit it. They are not a grant of a later legal status called full citizenship.

The inside of Yathrib is a haram for the people of this document. Whoever goes out is safe and whoever stays is safe, except one who does wrong or sins. Whatever they differ about is referred to God and to Muhammad. That referral is what the text says. It is not described here as a supreme constitutional court.

The sahifah is an early community agreement, preserved in the sirah and in Kitab al-Amwal. Later writers have compared it with constitutions and with modern ideas of equal citizenship. Those comparisons are interpretations. They are not clauses of the document, and this chapter does not state them as facts of the first year.
